quotes.quote: Common fusion methods include simple linear layers ... and attention mechanisms
Compared to linear layers, attention mechanisms can capture more complex inter-modal interactions, albeit at the cost of higher computational demands.
A linear projection layer bridges the gap between the visual encoder and the LLM.
fed into the video Q-Former. The video Q-Former extracts features from all frames
connected via a window-level Query Transformer in order to transform the encoder outputs

requirements.rationale: Evidence contrasts linear projections vs attention/Q-Former connectors and notes attention’s higher compute cost, but it does not explicitly declare a single lightweight speed ‘winner’. Hence only partial coverage of which connector is best for speed.
No chunk identifies specific models as ‘hallucination prone’ or discusses systematic hallucination behavior for particular backbones or connectors.

quotes.quote: taking approximately 10 hours on 4 A100 GPUs.
This fine-tuning is computationally efficient, taking only around 7 minutes with a single A100 GPU.
attention mechanisms can capture more complex inter-modal interactions, albeit at the cost of higher computational demands.
more lightweight model designs that significantly reduce computational overhead while maintaining performance

requirements.rationale: There are GPU/time compute hints and notes that attention-based connectors increase computational demands, but no explicit VRAM numbers or a clear breakdown of which components dominate VRAM in audio, video, or image pipelines.
OCR-free reading or similar capabilities are not mentioned; there is no evaluation of whether such features work well versus being marketing claims.

quotes.quote: it utilizes Vicuna as the language decoder, which is built upon LLaMA
NeXT-GPT achieves superior video quality with smaller parameter sizes (7B/13B).
Mini-Gemini excels as a lightweight model advantageous in resource-constrained or fast inference scenarios
smaller, more targeted models can deliver superior performance in specific domains.
LLM uses the Meta AI LLaMA model to sense multimodal inputs and generate multimodal outputs

requirements.rationale: Several backbones (LLaMA/Vicuna, NeXT-GPT 7B/13B, Mini-Gemini) are discussed with pros like smaller size or lightweight inference, but the review does not clearly crown a single dominating backbone across modalities such as Qwen vs Llama vs Vicuna.
Licensing or commercial vs research-only usage of any model is not discussed in the retrieved chunks.

quotes.quote: Both the language and vision models are open-sourced.
instruction tuning by a Low-Rank Adaptive Approach (LoRA)
this model also applies LoRA ... to further update the LLM’s parameters.

requirements.rationale: MiniGPT-4 explicitly uses open-sourced language and vision models, and SALMONN and NeXT-GPT apply LoRA for adaptation. However, the survey does not systematically list which other models have open weights or clarify closed-weight status, so coverage is only partial.

risks: Lack of hallucination analysis (R2) may lead to choosing backbones that fabricate content without awareness.
Absence of VRAM specifics (R3) risks underestimating hardware needs for deployment.
No discussion of OCR-free reading reliability (R4) could cause overreliance on unproven features.
Missing licensing details (R6) may result in selecting models unsuitable for commercial use.
Incomplete view of open vs closed weights (R7) may hinder future fine-tuning and customization plans.

coverage.notes: Connector tradeoffs, some backbone choices, and LoRA-based adaptation are reasonably covered, but hallucination behavior, licensing, OCR-free reading, and precise VRAM requirements are absent. The review supports qualitative architecture selection but not several critical operational and legal requirements.

redundancy.notes: Multiple chunks reiterate high-level benefits of MLLMs and general architecture patterns without adding requirement-specific details, while connector and backbone information is spread across several overlapping chunks.

budget_efficiency.notes: Some high-cost chunks provide strong architectural insight (e.g., Video-LLaMA, NeXT-GPT), but others with high cognitive cost mainly offer broad survey context rather than directly addressing the specific requirements.

risk_flags: Key deployment constraints like VRAM usage and component-wise memory drivers are not quantified, risking misestimation of hardware needs.
No hallucination-proneness analysis may lead to unsafe backbone choices for critical applications.
Licensing information is absent, posing legal and commercial-use risks.
Marketing claims such as OCR-free reading cannot be validated from the retrieved evidence.
Redundant high-level survey chunks consumed budget without improving coverage of the specific requirements.

quotes.quote: Common fusion methods include simple linear layers and attention mechanisms.
A linear projection layer bridges the gap between the visual encoder and the LLM.
The modules involved in the training of Video-LLaMA include the Video Q-Former, Audio Q-Former.
The outputs of the two auditory encoders are connected via a window-level Query Transformer.
Only the Transformer-based projection layers in the encoding and decoding stages are trainable.
Early Fusion: Combines input data at the initial stage.
Late Fusion: Integrates the final outputs from individual modal pathways at the decision stage.
This stage spans 20,000 training steps with a batch size of 256, taking approximately 10 hours on 4 A100 GPUs.
NeXT-GPT achieves superior video quality with smaller parameter sizes (7B/13B).
There is an ongoing debate about whether MLLMs should pursue a “big and comprehensive” approach or a “small and specialized” one.

decisions.decision: Architecture Selection: Choosing the Best 'Connector' and LLM Backbone.

answer.R1: The text contrasts linear projections vs attention/Q-Former/Transformer connectors and notes linear layers are lighter weight, but it does not name a specific 'lightweight winner' for speed among visual connectors like Q-Former vs projection. So the winner is unknown.
answer.R2: No models are explicitly described as 'hallucination prone' or making things up; this information is unknown.
answer.R3: VRAM requirements are not given. Only training time/GPU count for MiniGPT-4 is reported, without memory figures or a breakdown of which components dominate VRAM in audio/video/image. Unknown.
answer.R4: OCR-free reading is not mentioned; there is no evaluation of such a feature. Unknown.
answer.R5: The survey discusses a tension between big vs small models and mentions several backbones (LLaMA/Vicuna, Mini-Gemini, LWM, NeXT-GPT) but does not identify a single dominating backbone across modalities like Qwen vs Llama vs Vicuna. No clear overall winner is named.
answer.R6: Licensing or commercial vs research-only use is not discussed. Unknown.
answer.R7: Several models use open weights and LoRA-style adaptation: MiniGPT-4 uses open-sourced vision and language models with a trainable linear projection; SALMONN and NeXT-GPT apply LoRA on top of mostly frozen LLMs. The text does not systematically list which are closed vs open, but it confirms that MiniGPT-4’s components are open-sourced and that LoRA-based adaptation is used in SALMONN and NeXT-GPT.

decisions.notes: R1: Linear vs attention/Q-Former tradeoffs are described, but no explicit speed ranking among visual connectors. R2: No mention of hallucination behavior. R3: Only GPU counts and times for MiniGPT-4; no VRAM or component-wise memory analysis. R4: OCR-free reading absent. R5: Discussion of big vs small and several backbones, but no declared dominant model across modalities. R6: Licensing not covered. R7: MiniGPT-4 explicitly states both language and vision models are open-sourced and uses a linear projection; SALMONN and NeXT-GPT use LoRA for adaptation, implying open-weight-style fine-tuning, but the text does not comprehensively classify all models’ openness.
